# Target

Properties of the machine the build targets.

```rux
pub struct Target {
    pub os: OperatingSystem;
    pub arch: Architecture;
    pub abi: ApplicationBinaryInterface;
    pub endian: Endianness;
    pub pointerBits: uint;
    pub dataModel: DataModel;
    pub objectFormat: ObjectFormat;
    pub triple: char8[..];
}
```

Every field is fixed when compiling begins. Reading one produces no runtime code, so a branch on a field is
decided while compiling and the untaken side is not emitted.

## Fields

| Name           | Type                         | Description                                                                         |
| -------------- | ---------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `os`           | `OperatingSystem`            | The operating system.                                                               |
| `arch`         | `Architecture`               | The processor architecture.                                                         |
| `abi`          | `ApplicationBinaryInterface` | The calling and layout conventions the target's code follows.                       |
| `endian`       | `Endianness`                 | The order the target stores a multi-byte value's bytes in.                          |
| `pointerBits`  | `uint`                       | How many bits a pointer occupies.                                                   |
| `dataModel`    | `DataModel`                  | The widths the target's C environment assigns to `long` and to a pointer.           |
| `objectFormat` | `ObjectFormat`               | The object-file format compiled code is emitted in.                                 |
| `triple`       | `char8[..]`                  | The canonical target name, spelled `<os>-<arch>`, which is what `--target` accepts. |

## Methods

<h3 id="has-feature"><code>HasFeature</code></h3>

```rux
pub func HasFeature(self: &Target, feature: TargetFeature) -> bool
```

Whether the build enables `feature` on this target.
`self` is borrowed and `feature` is read by value. Answered while compiling, so a branch on it emits only the
side that applies and a body using an instruction the feature provides is never emitted without it.
Cannot fail: a feature the target does not have is absent rather than an error. Costs nothing in the built
program.

| Name      | Type            | Description                     |
| --------- | --------------- | ------------------------------- |
| `feature` | `TargetFeature` | the target feature to ask about |

**Returns**: whether the target being built for has it

[Source](https://github.com/rux-lang/Rux/blob/main/Packages/Core/Src/Target.rux#L145)

## Related

<h3 id="operating-system"><code>OperatingSystem</code></h3>

```rux
pub enum OperatingSystem: uint8 {
    Unknown = 0,
    FreeBSD = 1,
    Linux = 2,
    macOS = 3,
    Windows = 4
}
```

An operating system a build can target.
Named per system rather than per family, so a package can tell FreeBSD from Linux where their interfaces differ.

[Source](https://github.com/rux-lang/Rux/blob/main/Packages/Core/Src/Target.rux#L12)

**Cases**

| Name      | Value | Description                                                                 |
| --------- | ----- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Unknown` | `0`   | A target the compiler has no name for, which no supported build produces.   |
| `FreeBSD` | `1`   | FreeBSD. Told apart from the other BSDs, which this enumeration also names. |
| `Linux`   | `2`   | Linux, any distribution.                                                    |
| `macOS`   | `3`   | Apple macOS.                                                                |
| `Windows` | `4`   | Microsoft Windows.                                                          |

<h3 id="application-binary-interface"><code>ApplicationBinaryInterface</code></h3>

```rux
pub enum ApplicationBinaryInterface: uint8 {
    Unknown = 0,
    AAPCS64 = 1,
    SystemV = 2,
    WindowsX64 = 3
}
```

The calling and layout conventions a target's code follows.
This is what decides how arguments are passed and how aggregates are laid out, so a declaration that has to match
a foreign interface branches on it rather than on the operating system.

[Source](https://github.com/rux-lang/Rux/blob/main/Packages/Core/Src/Target.rux#L41)

**Cases**

| Name         | Value | Description                                                             |
| ------------ | ----- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Unknown`    | `0`   | An ABI the compiler has no name for, which no supported build produces. |
| `AAPCS64`    | `1`   | The AArch64 procedure call standard.                                    |
| `SystemV`    | `2`   | The System V AMD64 ABI, used by Linux, FreeBSD, and macOS on x86-64.    |
| `WindowsX64` | `3`   | The Windows x64 calling convention.                                     |

<h3 id="target-feature"><code>TargetFeature</code></h3>

```rux
pub enum TargetFeature: uint8 {
    AVX = 0,
    AVX2 = 1,
    AVX512 = 2,
    NEON = 3,
    SSE2 = 4,
    SSE3 = 5,
    SSE41 = 6,
    SSE42 = 7,
    SSSE3 = 8,
    SVE = 9
}
```

A processor feature a target may be built with.
Presence is asked about with [`Target::HasFeature`](/docs/api/core/target#has-feature) rather than read as a field, because a build enables a set
rather than a single one.

[Source](https://github.com/rux-lang/Rux/blob/main/Packages/Core/Src/Target.rux#L56)

**Cases**

| Name     | Value | Description                                   |
| -------- | ----- | --------------------------------------------- |
| `AVX`    | `0`   | x86 Advanced Vector Extensions.               |
| `AVX2`   | `1`   | x86 Advanced Vector Extensions 2.             |
| `AVX512` | `2`   | x86 Advanced Vector Extensions 512.           |
| `NEON`   | `3`   | Arm Advanced SIMD.                            |
| `SSE2`   | `4`   | x86 Streaming SIMD Extensions 2.              |
| `SSE3`   | `5`   | x86 Streaming SIMD Extensions 3.              |
| `SSE41`  | `6`   | x86 Streaming SIMD Extensions 4.1.            |
| `SSE42`  | `7`   | x86 Streaming SIMD Extensions 4.2.            |
| `SSSE3`  | `8`   | x86 Supplemental Streaming SIMD Extensions 3. |
| `SVE`    | `9`   | Arm Scalable Vector Extension.                |

<h3 id="endianness"><code>Endianness</code></h3>

```rux
pub enum Endianness: uint8 {
    Big = 0,
    Little = 1
}
```

The order a target stores a multi-byte value's bytes in.

[Source](https://github.com/rux-lang/Rux/blob/main/Packages/Core/Src/Target.rux#L81)

**Cases**

| Name     | Value | Description                                                                |
| -------- | ----- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Big`    | `0`   | Most significant byte first, which is network byte order.                  |
| `Little` | `1`   | Least significant byte first, which every currently supported target uses. |

<h3 id="data-model"><code>DataModel</code></h3>

```rux
pub enum DataModel: uint8 {
    Unknown = 0,
    LLP64 = 1,
    LP64 = 2
}
```

The widths a target's C environment assigns to `long` and to a pointer.
This is what a raw C declaration needs to get `long` right, since the two models disagree about it.

[Source](https://github.com/rux-lang/Rux/blob/main/Packages/Core/Src/Target.rux#L91)

**Cases**

| Name      | Value | Description                                                              |
| --------- | ----- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `Unknown` | `0`   | A model the compiler has no name for, which no supported build produces. |
| `LLP64`   | `1`   | 32-bit `long`, 64-bit pointer. Windows.                                  |
| `LP64`    | `2`   | 64-bit `long`, 64-bit pointer. Every supported Unix target.              |

pub enum ObjectFormat: uint8 {

<h3 id="target-constant"><code>#target</code></h3>

```rux
pub const #target: Target;
```

The machine being compiled for, as a compile-time value.
Reading a field produces no runtime code. A `when` on one keeps only the branch that applies, so the untaken side
is never resolved or type-checked and may name declarations this target does not have.

[Source](https://github.com/rux-lang/Rux/blob/main/Packages/Core/Src/Target.rux#L152)
